sweep_summary: yaka1269 (Kiyaka, Bantu H31) is not in the catalog. Of the 49 Glottolog 'prosody/phrasing' titles attached to it, only two are Yaka sources: Kidima 1991 'Tone and accent in KiYaka' (UCLA diss; Semantic Scholar record has no OA PDF, UCLA dissertation index 404s, Google Books/OpenAlex/HathiTrust quotas or bot-walls hit -- unread, HIGH priority) and Hyman 1998 'Positional prominence and the prosodic trough in Yaka' (already held by the project, read: a vowel-harmony paper; 'prominence' = stem-initial syllable segmental strength, p. 49; no word-stress statement). The other 47 titles are about other languages (German, French, Japanese, Korean, Chichewa, Greek, Irish, etc.) or general theory; OUP tables of contents for both Prosodic Typology volumes were read and contain no Bantu chapter. Two citing works were downloaded and saved (Jardine 2016 Phonology 33, which quotes Kidima 1991: 44 on tone plateauing and calls the analysis 'accentual'; Hyman 2013 PhonLab, Yaka only for nasal harmony). Hyman 2017 held by the project quotes Kidima 1990: 196: super-high = 'a High that surfaces on an accented vowel'. Downing 2004 'What African languages tell us about accent typology' (ZASPiL 37) was downloaded and has no Yaka mention; the Glottolog Downing 2004 TIE paper link is dead. Net: no first-hand stress-placement statement for Yaka exists in anything opened; Kidima 1991 and Kidima 1990 (Inkelas & Zec volume) remain the sources to acquire. ( appended).

tone_statements.citation: Hale, Kenneth and Selkirk, Elisabeth (1987). Government and tonal phrasing in Papago. Phonology Yearbook 4. pp. 151-184.
tone_statements.quote: As was mentioned earlier, KiYaka has three phonetic tones: L, H, and R. To account for the different surface tonal phenomena, I propose that KiYaka has basically the H-L opposition supplemented by accent. The H is specified underlyingly and can be prelinked or floating, but the L is supplied by default according to the following rule: … As for the R, I suggest that it is just the phonetic realisation of H on accented syllables. Specifically, the H is converted into R by the following phonetic rule. (13) H-RAISING: Realise an accented syllable linked to H as R.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 22-23, section 2.3.2 Accent; see also 2.1 Phonetic Tones p. 13 and 2.3.4.3 Rule Inventory pp. 47-48.
tone_statements.summary: Two-way tone contrast, H vs default L, plus a lexical accent (stem-initial, partly contrastive by mora) that raises a docked H to extra-high R; floating H tones donated rightward in the clitic group.

The text has zero occurrences of 'stress', 'accent', 'prominen-', 'penult', 'lengthen', 'Yaka' or 'Kiyaka' (63 occurrences of 'Bemba'). It describes Bemba, not Yaka, and says nothing about word stress even for Bemba. Not a Yaka source; silent on stress.

sources.quote: In Yaka (Kidima 1991), 'all toneless syllables flanked by Hs become H by rightward spreading of the H to the left of the domain' (Kidima 1991: 44). (19), from Kidima (1991: 180), shows plateauing alternations. Kidima gives Yaka tonal assignment a complex accentual analysis; the underlying Hs marked in the following data result from a tonal assignment rule.

sources.quote: The constraint IDENT V1 is designed to preserve the mora and features of the first stem syllable, which is known to be prominent in Bantu languages. [...] The greater prominence or 'strength' of both the consonants and vowels of stem-initial syllables is quite widespread in Benue-Congo languages (Hyman 1990). [p. 49] ... the account in (41) crucially depends on recognising the trough as a prosodically weak sequence occurring between two peaks of prominence. [p. 63]
sources.locator: p. 49 (constraint IDENT V1 and fn. 12); p. 63 (trough as weak sequence between two peaks of prominence)
sources.note: 'Prominence' here is positional/segmental (stem-initial syllable and final vowel preserve vowel contrasts; the stem-internal 'trough' is weak). The paper is about vowel harmony; it never states a word-stress or accent position for Yaka and does not use the word stress for Yaka.
